questions.prompt: Case c4: The password spray from 192.0.2.150 actually occurred. Why is the verdict Benign True Positive (BTP) rather than False Positive (FP)?

options.a: The rule mis-parsed the authentication logons
options.b: The claimed behavior genuinely occurred but was authorized under the Bluewater engagement letter
options.c: No user account was compromised, so it cannot be any kind of positive
options.d: The originating source IP is an internal network address

questions.prompt: Case c6: 64-second periodic traffic to 192.0.2.10:123. Why is the verdict False Positive (FP) rather than Benign True Positive (BTP)?

options.a: NTP traffic is authorized, and authorized activity is always FP
options.b: The 64-second interval is too short to qualify as C2 beaconing
options.c: BTP requires the rule's threat claim to accurately describe the behavior — here the traffic is NTP, so the C2 claim itself is wrong
options.d: UDP traffic cannot function as C2

questions.prompt: What action should closing an alert as Benign True Positive (BTP) produce?

options.a: An incident ticket escalated to Tier 2
options.c: Detection tuning feedback (e.g. allowlist the change window or authorized source IP) without an incident ticket
options.d: An immediate password reset for the involved account
